title: Why the vault is cold
task: Say what the cold and the drying are for.
scene: Mbaye has two lots of the same seed on the bench. One spent four years dried, at minus eighteen degrees. The other sat in a warm shed, and only three in ten still grow.
assumes: some seeds can survive being dried out and frozen
takeaway: Cold and dry do not stop a seed ageing. They slow it down.
question: Why does cold, dry storage keep a seed alive longer?
why: A dried seed is still alive, and being alive means chemistry going on inside it. That chemistry slowly damages the parts the seed will need when it wakes up. Taking the water out slows those changes down. Cold slows them further, so the two work together. It is not a fuel tank running out. It is damage adding up, and everything in the vault is there to make it add up more slowly.
answerText: Cold and drying slow the chemistry that damages a seed from the inside, so it stays able to grow for far longer.

choices: They slow down the chemical changes that damage a stored seed.
They keep the seed asleep, by blocking the signals that start it growing.
They mostly work by killing the moulds already in the packet.
They harden the seed coat, so the living cells inside need no repair.
rebuttals: Staying asleep stops a seed sprouting at the wrong time. It does not explain decades of slower ageing.
Drying and sealing do hold pests and mould back. A clean seed still ages.
The coat does not make the cells inside maintenance-free. What changes is how fast the damage builds up.

title: Two parents, and what you are asking of them
task: Say what the cross is for.
scene: Volpe has two parents pinned above the bench. One is a modern wheat that yields well. The other is an old local kind that came through the 2018 drought. Bengtsson asks what she wants.
assumes: young plants get half their genes from each parent
takeaway: A cross is a request for a combination, and it takes generations to find out whether it was granted.
question: What is the programme actually asking for by crossing these two?
why: Each parent hands on half its genes, so the first generation gets one set from each. The generation after that shuffles those sets into thousands of combinations. What the breeder wants is the yield genes of the modern parent together with the drought genes of the old one. Neither parent has that. Most of the offspring will be worse than either. Breeding is growing enough of them to find the rare ones worth keeping.
answerText: Plants carrying useful genes from both parents at once. Neither parent has that combination, which is why it takes generations.

choices: Plants that carry the useful genes of both parents at once.
Plants halfway between the two parents in everything.
An old local kind, improved by contact with the modern one.
A cross that beats both parents, because crosses are stronger.
rebuttals: Traits built from many genes do average out. The ones being chased here do not.
An old local kind is a whole population. Crossing changes what comes out of it rather than improving it in place.
Crosses do beat their parents in some crops, and that is not what this programme is for.

title: Why the same line is sown four times
task: Say what sowing each line four times buys.
scene: Meera Quiroga has the plot map on the wall. Two hundred and forty plots, each line sown four times across four blocks, in scrambled order. The north end is visibly wetter.
assumes: the same crop grows differently in different parts of a field
takeaway: A field is not the same all over, so one plot measures the ground as much as the seed in it.
question: What does sowing each line in four scattered plots buy?
why: Ground varies. Drainage, depth, shelter, how hard it was driven over. Sow a line once and its yield is the seed and that patch mixed together, with no way to tell them apart. Sow it four times in different blocks and the patches differ while the seed does not. Scrambling the order stops anybody's habits handing good ground to a favourite. How much the four disagree is itself a measure of how much the ground matters.
answerText: A comparison between seeds rather than between patches of ground — and a measure of how much the ground was worth.

choices: A comparison that separates the seed from the piece of ground it grew on.
Four separate lots of seed, protecting next season's planting stock.
Cover against one storm wiping out the whole trial.
A more exact yield figure from each individual plot.
rebuttals: A yield trial is harvested to compare. These four are not four separate seed stocks.
Weather arrives across the whole site, so four nearby plots are not four separate seasons.
Each plot is measured the same way. What repeating buys is a better comparison, not a better plot.

title: Counting a generation
task: Say what the counts show about the resistance.
scene: Four hundred plants from the second generation. Three hundred and six shrug the disease off, and ninety-four do not. Bengtsson asks what that number was supposed to be.
assumes: a plant carries two copies of each gene and passes on one of them
takeaway: The proportions across a whole generation carry information that no single plant does.
question: What do 306 resistant and 94 not tell you about this resistance?
why: The first generation carried one resistant copy and one that is not. Each parent passes on one copy at random, so three in four of their children get at least one resistant copy. In four hundred plants that is three hundred resistant and a hundred not. The count came in at 306 and 94, which is as close as counting ever gets. Two genes, with either one enough, would predict 375 and 25 instead.
answerText: One gene, with the resistant copy winning. Three in four of four hundred is three hundred, and the count came in at 306.

choices: One gene is doing it, and the resistant copy wins when both are present.
Two genes are doing it, and either one of them is enough.
The resistance is partly the glasshouse rather than the plants.
The test used to pick the parents was wrong.
rebuttals: Two genes, with either one enough, gives about one plant in sixteen falling ill. Not one in four.
The bay is infected deliberately. A plant can escape, and that would not give a clean pattern.
A wrong test in the parents would break the pattern rather than produce a textbook one.

title: One disagreement, two possible causes
task: Fit the disagreement both ways, then use the direct gene test to separate them.
scene: Nakagawa has four hundred plants scored two ways: by a DNA test, and by whether they fell ill. Eleven carry the marker and still fell ill. The test's own controls look clean.
assumes: a DNA test looks for a chosen stretch of DNA
a marker sits near a gene rather than inside it
a plant swaps pieces between its two copies of a chromosome when it makes seed
takeaway: A test can be right about the marker and still be wrong about the plant.
question: Which mixes of swapping and test error fit the disagreement, and which one survives the direct gene test?
why: The DNA test here does not look at the resistance gene. It looks at a marker sitting near it. Near is not inside. When a plant makes seed, its two copies of a chromosome swap pieces, and a marker close to a gene usually travels with it and sometimes does not. So eleven disagreements could be swapping, or a test that misreads. One number cannot separate those two. A second test aimed at the gene itself can.
answerText: The first result fits several mixes of swapping and test error. Testing the gene itself rules out the misreading, and swapping is what is left — about four plants in a hundred.

title: Where a tonne of grain comes from
task: Say where the weight in the harvest came from.
scene: Toft has eleven tonnes of grain from one field on the weighbridge slip. A trainee has just said the crop got it out of the soil. He would like that settled.
assumes: plants build sugars out of carbon dioxide and water, using light
takeaway: A harvest weighs what it weighs because of something that was not there when it started.
question: Where does almost all the dry weight of that grain come from?
why: Nearly all the dry weight of grain is carbohydrate, and the carbon in it walked in through the leaves as carbon dioxide. Light supplies the energy and water supplies the rest, and the plant builds sugars out of the two. Those sugars become stem, root and grain. Water moves through the plant in enormous amounts and leaves again as vapour. Minerals decide how much can be built, rather than what it is built from.
answerText: Almost all of it came out of the air, as carbon dioxide taken in through the leaves.

choices: Carbon dioxide, taken out of the air through the leaves.
Minerals, taken out of the soil by the roots.
Water, taken out of the soil by the roots.
The nitrogen fertiliser spread in the spring.
rebuttals: Minerals matter, and they are a few per cent of the dry weight at most.
Water is most of a living plant, and nearly all of it has gone by the time grain is dry.
Nitrogen changes how much the crop can build. What it adds to the weight is small.

title: What a season costs
task: Say what holding the release back really costs.
scene: Volpe has the pipeline on the board. Cross to release is seven years, and everything behind WM-712 moves back with it. Qureshi asks what a year of a wheat variety is worth.
assumes: a breeding programme moves one generation at a time
takeaway: The cost of holding something back is rarely paid by the thing being held back.
question: Why does holding it one season cost more than one season?
why: A breeding programme is a queue sharing the same seasons, the same ground and the same people. Hold this line for a year and its seed increase waits. So does the trial that would have used that ground, and the crosses behind it. The bill lands on lines that were never part of the argument. That does not settle whether releasing is right. It makes the price of waiting something everybody can see.
answerText: Everything behind it waits too. One season of delay is paid for by lines that had nothing to do with the argument.

choices: Everything behind it in the queue waits as well.
The line loses its edge as everybody else's wheat improves.
Seed held for a year does not grow as well afterwards.
The trial results go out of date and have to be repeated.
rebuttals: Other wheat does improve, slowly, and that is not what makes one season expensive.
A year in a cold store costs a well-dried sample almost nothing.
Trial results do not go out of date. They become another year in the series.

title: What the trial can actually claim
task: Say what four seasons of trials support.
scene: Four seasons, one site, four plots each. WM-712 is ahead by eleven per cent in the two dry years and by two in the wet ones. The leaflet says eleven per cent higher yielding.
assumes: a trial measures what happened under the conditions it happened in
takeaway: A number from a trial carries the conditions it was measured in, or it is a different claim.
question: What does this trial support saying about WM-712?
why: The eleven per cent belongs to two dry years on one farm. In the wet years it was two. Strip the conditions off and the sentence turns into a claim nobody tested. So the honest version carries its weather with it. This line did especially well in dry seasons, on this ground. That is a good reason to try it in other dry places, and it is not a substitute for doing so.
answerText: That its advantage here was far bigger in the two dry years than in the wet ones. Eleven per cent on its own is a different claim.

choices: At this site, its advantage is much bigger in dry seasons than in wet ones.
Across these four seasons it is eleven per cent better here, whatever the weather.
Its dry-year result shows it suits dry regions everywhere.
It should beat the standard whenever the rain is below average.
rebuttals: In the wet years the advantage was two per cent, so eleven is not a number that holds whatever the season.
One site can suggest that idea. It cannot test it anywhere else.
The trial separates dry years from wet ones here. It does not set a rainfall line that guarantees anything.

title: What the crop cannot do without water
task: Say why a dry summer costs yield.
scene: Toft has eleven years of yield against summer rain, and a roughly straight line through it. A trainee asks why a plant built out of air minds a dry summer at all.
assumes: plants take carbon dioxide in through tiny pores in their leaves
takeaway: The opening a leaf takes carbon in through is the opening it loses water through.
question: Why does drought cut the yield, when the weight comes from the air?
why: A leaf takes carbon dioxide in through pores, and water vapour goes out through the same pores. A crop loses far more water that way than it ever uses for building. When the soil dries, the plant closes those pores to hold on to the water. That saves the plant and shuts the carbon out, so the building stops. Drought brings other troubles as well. This is the trade that costs the yield.
answerText: Closing the pores to save water shuts the carbon dioxide out at the same time, so the crop stops building.

choices: Closing the pores to save water shuts the carbon dioxide out too.
The roots cannot take up the minerals the grain is built from.
The plant cannot keep itself cool, and the heat wrecks it.
Photosynthesis needs liquid water in large amounts as a raw material.
rebuttals: Taking up minerals does suffer in dry soil, and it is not the main road from drought to lost yield.
Heat damage is real, and it is a separate problem that often arrives at the same time.
The water actually used in photosynthesis is a tiny fraction of what the crop loses.

title: What came with the gene
task: Explain why the resistant plants are short.
scene: Every line carrying the resistance is twelve to fifteen centimetres shorter than its sisters without it. The parent it came from was short. The parent it was bred back into is tall.
assumes: genes sit in fixed places along a chromosome, in a fixed order
takeaway: A chromosome is passed on in stretches, so a wanted gene arrives with its neighbours.
question: Why are the resistant plants shorter?
why: Genes sit in a row along a chromosome, and a chromosome is handed on in stretches rather than gene by gene. So a gene you want arrives with whatever sits beside it. Here the resistance came from a short parent, and a piece of that parent's chromosome came with it. Splitting the two needs a swap in exactly that gap, which is rare. So you grow thousands, and look for the one plant where it happened.
answerText: The resistance arrived with a piece of the short parent's chromosome. Splitting them needs a rare swap in a very small gap.

choices: They carry the short parent's neighbouring genes along with the resistance.
Fighting off the disease costs the plant its growth.
Breeding back to one parent weakens the plants each time.
The short ones got picked by accident in the glasshouse.
rebuttals: Fighting a disease does cost a plant something, and not a steady fifteen centimetres.
Breeding back recovers the tall parent. It does not weaken anything by itself.
The picking in the bay was done on the DNA test. Nobody measured height at all.

title: A test fitted where it worked
task: Set the cut-off, freeze it, and score it on plants it has never seen.
scene: The DNA test was worked out on the first population, and it has picked plants right for three seasons. Nakagawa has a new cross, and a hundred plants scored both ways.
assumes: a test predicts a trait by sitting near the gene, in the population it was worked out on
takeaway: A rule fitted on one set of plants has to be scored on a set it has never seen.
question: Set the cut-off on the plants the test was worked out on. Then freeze it and score it on the new cross. What does it get?
why: A cut-off chosen on one population partly fits that population's accidents, and accidents do not have to repeat. A broad shelf of good scores is worth trusting. It survives being frozen and used on a new cross. A sharp peak at one exact value does not. That peak was fitted to noise. Scoring on plants the rule has never seen is the only way to tell the two apart.
answerText: About 94 per cent, from a cut-off near 48. The cut-off at 63 scores 99 on the old plants and 79 on the new cross, and twenty of those points were noise.

title: Short is not simply worse
task: Say what shorter plants do to the harvest.
scene: Toft points out that shorter wheats were the whole point of the 1960s. Less stem, more grain, and they stand up in the rain. Volpe still did not ask for fifteen centimetres.
assumes: a plant shares out what it builds between stem, leaf and grain
takeaway: What matters is the share of what a plant built that ends up in the grain.
question: Why can a shorter wheat outyield a taller one?
why: A plant builds a certain amount over a season, and then shares it out. A shorter wheat spends less of it on stem, so more can go into grain. Short stems also stay standing through wind and rain, and grain that stays upright is grain the combine can collect. That is why the short wheats of the 1960s changed everything. It does not follow that every short plant is better, which is exactly what Volpe still has to find out.
answerText: More of what it builds ends up in grain instead of stem — and short stems stay standing, so the grain can be collected.

choices: More of what it builds goes into grain rather than stem.
It builds faster than a tall plant does.
It uses less water, because there is less of it.
It keeps its leaves clear of the soil and dodges disease.
rebuttals: How fast a leaf works is not what height changes.
Water use follows leaf area and how long the season is, rather than how tall the stem is.
Lifting leaves away from soil spores does help with some diseases. It is not the yield story.

title: Not the number of plants
task: Work out what share of the plants gave pollen.
scene: Last year's grow-out used a hundred and twenty plants. Only eighteen of them gave pollen, and a hundred and two set seed. Ivanescu wants that looked at before the next plan.
assumes: this crop keeps pollen and seed on separate plants
every seed has one parent on each side
takeaway: A crowd of plants can pass on as little as a handful, if one side of the family is small.
question: What share of the plants gave pollen?
why: Every seed gets half its genes from a pollen plant and half from a seed plant. So the pollen side is a doorway that everything has to come through. Here that doorway was eighteen plants wide, out of a hundred and twenty standing in the plot. Fifteen per cent. What it costs is variety. Whatever those eighteen plants did not carry is gone from the batch, however many plants were standing there.
answerText: Fifteen per cent. Every seed in that batch got its pollen from one of just eighteen plants.

estimate.prompt: A hundred and twenty plants stood in the plot. Eighteen of them gave pollen, and a hundred and two set seed.
estimate.question: What share of the plants gave pollen?
estimate.relationship: Share = the pollen plants ÷ all the plants × 100.
estimate.explanation: A hundred and twenty plants stood there, and that is not the number that matters. Every seed had to get its pollen from one of eighteen.
estimate.solution: Eighteen ÷ a hundred and twenty, times a hundred, is fifteen per cent.

title: Write the rule before it falls
task: Set the thresholds before replaying the record.
scene: Mbaye has eleven germination tests on one batch, falling from ninety-eight per cent to eighty-five. The rule says grow it out at eighty-five. Booking a field takes time, and so does the grow-out.
assumes: germination is the share of seeds that actually grow
a grow-out needs field space booked before it can start
takeaway: A threshold has to fire early enough for the thing it starts to arrive in time.
question: Where should each threshold sit, so the grow-out is ready before the seed drops below the floor?
why: The floor is where the seed stops being good enough. It is the wrong moment to start planning, because everything you would do next takes time. Booking a field takes several updates. Starting the grow-out takes another. Set the thresholds before the numbers arrive, and hindsight cannot quietly move them later. Reserve at ninety and start at eighty-six, and both land in time. Wait for eighty-five and the work begins after the line has been crossed.
answerText: Reserve the field at ninety per cent and start the grow-out at eighty-six. Waiting for eighty-five is too late, once the time each step takes is counted.

title: A difference that was the field
task: Say why last year's height difference has gone.
scene: Last season two pure lines differed by nine centimetres in height, clearly. This season the same lines went onto different plots, and now they do not differ at all. The seed has not changed.
assumes: the same line grown in two places can give two different answers
takeaway: A result that does not survive being grown somewhere else was probably about the somewhere.
question: What is the most likely explanation?
why: One season's comparison holds the seed, and whatever was odd about the plots each line got. Scrambling the layout makes deliberate favouring unlikely. One layout can still be lucky. Growing them again on new ground asks whether the difference follows the seed. Here it did not. So last year's nine centimetres was mostly the ground. This is what growing things twice is for.
answerText: Last year's difference was mostly the plots. It did not follow the seed onto new ground, so it was not the seed.

choices: Last year's difference was partly the plots those lines landed on.
The lines have changed between one season and the next.
This year's measurements were taken less carefully.
Height is not passed on in wheat.
rebuttals: Pure lines do not change in a single season.
Careless measuring adds scatter. It does not remove a nine-centimetre difference.
Height is strongly passed on, which is exactly why this disappearance is worth explaining.

title: What one round returns
task: Predict what the next generation will average.
scene: The trial averages 7.4 tonnes a hectare. The twenty plots Volpe wants to keep average 9.1. Quiroga says about a third of that head start gets passed on.
assumes: a plant's performance is partly what it inherited and partly where it grew
takeaway: Only the inherited share of an advantage is passed on, and for yield that share is small.
question: What should the next generation average?
why: The plots you choose are above average for two reasons. Some of it is the plants, and some of it is the ground they happened to stand on. Only the first travels to the next generation. Here the head start is 1.7 tonnes, and about three tenths of that is inherited, so the gain is roughly half a tonne. Expect 9.1 next year and the disappointment is guaranteed. Expect 7.9 and the programme is honest with itself.
answerText: About 7.9 tonnes a hectare — a gain of half a tonne, rather than the full 1.7.

estimate.prompt: The trial averages 7.4 tonnes a hectare and the chosen plots average 9.1. About three tenths of that head start is inherited.
estimate.question: What should the next generation average?
estimate.relationship: Next average = the trial average + three tenths of the head start.
estimate.explanation: The chosen plots are 1.7 above average, and most of that was the ground they stood on. Only the inherited share travels.
givens: The trial averages 7.4 and the chosen plots 9.1
About 0.3 of the head start is inherited

title: An extra generation in the bay
task: Decide what the extra generation is for.
scene: Bengtsson can run one more generation over the winter in the warm bay. A generation there takes three months instead of twelve. There is room for one population.
assumes: a glasshouse can finish a generation out of season
takeaway: A generation indoors is for moving material along, not for judging it.
question: What should the warm bay be used for this winter?
why: The warm bay is worth most when time is the thing in short supply. Splitting the resistance from the short-stem genes needs more generations, because each one is another chance at a rare swap. So that work uses the bay well. A yield figure from a glasshouse means nothing, because no field is like a glasshouse. Regrowing an old kind in there would quietly select for whatever suits a glasshouse. Multiplying seed needs area, which the bay has least of.
answerText: Advancing the backcross. It buys another generation and another chance at the rare swap, without pretending a glasshouse can stand in for a field.

choices: Advancing the backcross that needs a rare swap.
Yield-testing the twenty chosen lines early.
Growing out the old kind that is overdue.
Multiplying seed of WM-712 for the merchant.
rebuttals: A yield figure from a glasshouse is measured under conditions no field ever offers.
Regrowing an old kind under glass selects for whatever suits a glasshouse, and nobody chose that.
Multiplying seed needs area, and the bay is the smallest ground on the station.

title: Why those two did well
task: Say what explains the best two plots.
scene: Two of the twenty chosen plots covered the ground eleven days before the rest and flowered four days earlier. Their yields are the best in the trial, and the season went dry after flowering.
assumes: a crop builds most of its grain from light caught after it flowers
takeaway: An early crop catches light while there is still water to use it with.
question: Why did the early lines yield best in this season?
why: A crop's yield comes down to three things. How much light it catches, how well it turns that into growth, and how much of the growth reaches the grain. This season the water ran out after flowering. The two lines that covered the ground early caught more light while their pores could still stay open. They also filled their grain in the wetter half. That is dodging this weather.
answerText: They caught their light and filled their grain before the water ran out. In a wet year that head start could vanish.

choices: They caught the light and set their grain before the soil dried out.
Flowering early makes each leaf work harder.
They dodged the rust, which arrived late.
Early cover shades the weeds out.
rebuttals: How hard a leaf works is not what flowering date changes.
The rust came nowhere near this trial, and dodging it would show as health rather than yield.
Shading weeds out is a real gain from early cover, and it is not worth this much yield.

title: Which evidence shares the grow-out
task: Open what each result rests on, keep what stands alone, and name what the rest share.
scene: Thirty of ninety batches no longer match their records from the 1990s. Nakagawa has four kinds of evidence on the board. The shelf checks are clean.
assumes: a result can depend on how something was handled, as well as on today's test
evidence is only independent if it does not share the important step
takeaway: Several results can agree because they share one history, and that is not several reasons.
question: Which results inherit the repeated small grow-outs, and which stand apart from them?
why: Three of the four kinds of evidence rest on the same grow-out history, so their agreement is one cause counted three times. The germination evidence does not. It rests on tests of whether the seed grows, and it says the seed is fine. Opening what each one depends on splits the story in two. The store kept the seed alive. The grow-outs changed what was in it. Throwing out the germination evidence would lose the half that stands alone.
answerText: The genetic results all share the repeated grow-outs. Keep the germination evidence. It shows the store did its job.

title: What the screen may not find
task: Say what the drift does to the screen.
scene: Nakagawa is screening fifty batches for a second resistance gene. Twenty-two of them are on the drifted list, and their test controls are clean. She wants to know what a clean result still means.
assumes: a gene that is rare in a population may be missing from a small sample of it
takeaway: A screen finds what is in front of it, and what is in front of it is what survived the last grow-out.
question: What does the drift mean for the screen?
why: Drift can remove a gene that was rare to begin with. So a clean result from one of those batches has two explanations. The gene was never there, or it was there and got lost in a grow-out. The test cannot tell those apart, because it is looking at the seed in front of it. A positive is still worth having, because drift removes genes and never invents them. The fix is to test material that missed the bottleneck.
answerText: A clean result no longer proves the gene was never there. It may have been lost in a grow-out, and the test cannot tell the difference.

choices: A clean result on those batches no longer proves the gene is absent.
The screen will report genes that are not there, on the drifted material.
The screen has to be rebuilt around different tests.
Nothing. Resistance genes get kept, because they are useful.
rebuttals: Drift removes genes rather than inventing them, so a positive result is unaffected.
The tests work. What has changed is the seed they are being run on.
Nothing in a vault cares about rust, so there is no reason for resistance to be kept.

title: What the store did right
task: Name the step that failed.
scene: Qureshi wants one sentence for the board. It has to name what failed, rather than the room it happened near. The vault log covers twenty-eight years with no fault.
assumes: a store keeps what it is given rather than improving it
takeaway: Storage held what it was handed. The loss happened in the field, on the way back in.
question: What is the honest statement of what went wrong?
why: The fix depends on naming the step that failed. The vault kept the seed cold, and the seed still grows. What changed tracks the number of grow-outs, where a few plants stood in for a whole population. Call it a storage failure and money goes to freezers that already worked. Call it a grow-out failure and attention goes where it belongs. The same packet can hold healthy seed and be a poor copy of what it came from.
answerText: Storage kept the seed alive. Repeated small grow-outs changed what was in it, by letting too few plants be the parents.

choices: Storage kept the seed alive, while repeated grow-outs changed what was in it.
The old records are too rough for any comparison of this kind.
The testing method has drifted over the years and invented the difference.
Seed died in store, and that decided which plants survived.
rebuttals: The old records predict the less-regrown batches correctly, so their roughness is not the pattern.
Controls and archived comparisons show no drift in the method that follows the number of grow-outs.
The affected packets still grow well, and death in store would follow storage history rather than grow-outs.

title: Which one is worth the slot
task: Spend the two checks on evidence that could change which batch gets the slot.
scene: Two of the fifty batches carry a different resistance gene, and the screenhouse can grow only one of them this season. One vial looks thin, the other is full.
assumes: a grow-out can change what is in a batch, by chance
a small lot of living seed can often be built back up
takeaway: The best measurement is the one that could change the decision, not the one with the most detail in it.
question: Which evidence is worth buying before the slot is committed?
why: The question is not which vial has more seed in it today. A thin vial with living seed can be built back up in one careful season. What cannot be repaired is a batch that has already lost what made it worth keeping. So the check worth buying is the one that says which batch has been through grow-outs and which has not. Another round of the same test would add detail and change nothing.
answerText: Buy the grow-out history. Then take the batch that has never been regrown — eleven grams is about three hundred seeds, which is plenty to build up.

title: What was lost, and when
task: Work out what happened to the resistance in this batch.
scene: Ivanescu has the 1994 field notes for the drifted batch. The collector saw rust on the crop, and noted that about one plant in twenty stayed clean. Today's sample has none.
assumes: something rare in a population can be missed altogether when a few plants are taken
takeaway: A gene that has vanished was not necessarily destroyed. It may only have failed to be picked.
why: The 1994 note says about one plant in twenty stayed clean. So the resistance was there, and it was rare. Take thirty plants at random from a crop where one in twenty carries something, and there is a real chance of taking none. Do that three times and losing it altogether gets likely. Nothing in a clean nursery gives a resistant plant any advantage, so nothing was holding on to it.
answerText: Lost by chance, across three small grow-outs. The old note shows the resistance was rare, and rare things get missed when only a few plants are taken.

choices: Chance removed it across three small grow-outs.
The 1994 collector wrote it down wrongly.
The grow-outs actively selected against it.
It is still there, and the test cannot see it here.
choiceMechanisms: Something in one plant in twenty can easily be missed when thirty are taken, three times over.
A mistaken note would not fit the rest of that collecting trip.
Selecting against a gene needs something acting on it, and the nurseries had no rust in them.
A failed test would show in the controls, and the controls came out right.
text.headline: The 1994 notes describe resistant plants in this batch. Today's sample has none.

title: The copy that was never in the vault
task: Say why the farm may hold what the vault lost.
scene: Fenn's old wheats are growing in the station plots. His family has grown one of them without a break since before Wellmere existed. Rust arrives there most years.
assumes: a crop growing where a disease turns up is being tested by it every year
takeaway: A population kept in the ground keeps being tested by the thing you might one day need it for.
question: Why is Fenn's field likely to hold what the vault lost?
why: Rust has come through Fenn's field most years. In a rust year the plants that shrug it off set more seed, and their share of the next crop goes up. Nobody planned that. It happens because the disease is there. The vault's grow-outs were done in clean nurseries, where resistance bought a plant nothing, so anything rare could quietly vanish. His field is not a frozen copy of 1994. It may be better than one.
answerText: Rust has tested his crop every year the vault stood still. What survives a test keeps being there; what is never tested can drift away.

choices: Rust has tested it every year the vault stood still.
His seed is fresher, so it is more complete.
He has more seed than the vault has of that batch.
Farm-saved seed changes faster than stored seed.
rebuttals: Freshness decides whether seed grows. It says nothing about which genes are in it.
Quantity is not the problem. The vault has plenty of a population that has lost the gene.
New genes appear far too rarely to put one back in thirty years.

title: Eight crossing commitments
task: Spend the eight slots, and keep both resistance questions answered.
scene: The crossing board has eight slots for the next two years. Volpe wants yield crosses. Qureshi wants new resistance brought in. The elite line still needs the second gene.
assumes: a cross ties up glasshouse space and staff for several seasons
closely related parents share the same weaknesses
takeaway: A breeding plan is the set of questions it chooses to answer, and every slot spent delays another.
question: Which packages keep the programme defended without spending the board on work that can wait?
why: There are two urgent questions and eight slots. One is getting the second resistance gene into the wheat farmers already grow. The other is getting it into unrelated wheat, so the programme does not rebuild the same weak point. Yield crosses between elite parents are useful, and they narrow the same base further. Fenn's plants will not be understood for two seasons. Spend the board on what cannot wait.
answerText: Fund the second-gene backcross and the two unrelated crosses. That is six of the eight slots, and it answers both urgent questions.

title: How narrow the base has become
task: Say what the pedigree board shows about the programme.
scene: Ivanescu has six elite parents' family trees across the wall. Four share a recent grandparent. All six carry the same resistance gene, and the new rust is beating it east of here.
assumes: related parents share more of their genes than unrelated ones do
takeaway: A programme that keeps crossing its best with its best is narrowing what it can still draw on.
question: What is the risk in the current elite parents?
why: Related parents share more of the same genes. So crossing best with best, over and over, leaves fewer different genes to choose from later. That is the slow problem. The fast one is sharper. All six of these parents carry the same resistance gene, and that gene is being beaten now. There is no back-up sitting in the programme. Bringing in unrelated wheat rebuilds the choices.
answerText: A narrow set of choices, and one shared weak point — every parent carries the resistance gene that is now failing.

choices: A narrow set of choices, plus one resistance gene shared by all six.
Serious weakening, because four parents share a recent grandparent.
No room left to improve yield by choosing among their offspring.
Faster loss of seed in store, because related parents store alike.
rebuttals: Wheat pollinates itself and copes with close relatives. The problem is a short list of alternatives.
A narrow base slows progress. It does not make choosing impossible.
How long seed lasts depends on how it was dried and stored, not on whose grandparent it shares.

title: Gene present, resistance working?
task: Decide what gets tested early, and what the finished line must still show.
scene: Nakagawa can run the DNA test on two-leaf seedlings. On final plants she can also check whether the gene is switched on after rust, and put real rust on the leaves.
assumes: a nearby marker can come apart from the gene it stands for
a gene has to be switched on before it does anything
takeaway: DNA says what a plant carries. Only a real test says whether it works.
question: Which evidence belongs early, and what must the final line still prove?
why: The DNA test is worth running early, because it clears out most seedlings months before rust could be used. It is not proof. The marker sits near the gene rather than inside it, and the two can come apart. Even the gene itself only says what the plant carries. It has to switch that gene on when rust arrives. So the last plants get real rust put on them.
answerText: Use the DNA test early to clear seedlings. Then make the final line show the gene switching on, and shrug off real rust.

choices: Use the DNA test early. On the final line, check it switches on and beats real rust.
Check the switching every generation. The final rust test is then unnecessary.
Put rust on every generation. Use the DNA test only after the last backcross.
Use the DNA test early and late. Carrying the gene is enough.
rebuttals: Switching on is worth knowing, and the plant still has to beat the rust in the end.
Waiting for real rust every generation throws away the months the DNA test buys.
A nearby marker can come apart from the gene, and carrying a gene does not prove it works.

title: What the catalogue says and what is there
task: Say what the season established about the collection.
scene: Ninety batches were tested. Thirty had changed, and every one of those had been regrown at least twice. The sixty regrown once or never still match. Nine thousand batches have been regrown twice or more.
assumes: a sample can support a statement about the group it came from
takeaway: A sample can point at a risky group without proving how many in it are affected.
question: What can Wellmere honestly say to its board on Monday?
why: The sample splits cleanly on one thing: how often a batch was regrown. All thirty of the repeatedly regrown ones had changed, and the sixty others had not. That is strong evidence that regrowing is what marks a batch as risky. It does not license saying a third of the whole collection has changed, because the two groups had different histories. Nor does thirty batches prove that all nine thousand are affected.
answerText: That repeated regrowing marks the risky group. Audit those first and change the method now, while a bigger sample says how common it is.

choices: Repeatedly regrown batches are the risky group, and should be audited first.
About a third of the whole forty-one thousand has changed.
Only the thirty tested batches can be treated as affected.
All nine thousand regrown batches should be assumed to have changed.
rebuttals: The one-third figure mixes batches with very different histories, so it cannot be spread across the collection.
The sample points beyond the thirty packets, even though it cannot name every affected batch.
All thirty tested ones had changed, and thirty is not enough to claim every one of nine thousand has.

title: One site, one year, again
task: Say how the season's result should be written up.
scene: The trial is scored and the lines are chosen. The summary goes to a board that will remember one number. It was a dry season, at one site.
assumes: a trial's conclusions belong to the conditions it ran under
takeaway: The sentence worth writing is the one that survives being quoted on its own.
question: How should this season's result be summarised?
why: Strip the conditions off a yield number and it turns into a claim nobody tested. This season's gain belongs to one site in a dry year. The chosen plots are worse still as a headline. They were picked after the results were seen, so their advantage includes lucky ground. Putting the site and the season in the same sentence is not caution. It is what the number means.
answerText: Report the trial-wide gain with the dry season and the site in the same sentence. Those conditions are part of the number.

choices: Report the trial-wide gain, with the dry season and site in the same sentence.
Report the bigger figure from the chosen plots, since those lines go forward.
Report the trial-wide gain as the headline, and put the conditions in a footnote.
Hold the result back until another season gives the same number.
rebuttals: The chosen plots were picked after the results were seen, so their advantage includes lucky ground.
A headline travels without its footnote, and turns a conditional result into a general one.
A second season tests how far the result travels. The first season's result is still real.

title: Twelve years, and what they are for
task: Say what the long record is worth keeping for.
scene: Toft's records of cover, flowering and weather now run to twelve seasons. Nobody has ever asked for the whole series. This year two of them explained why the best plots pulled away.
assumes: a long record lets one season be compared against the others
takeaway: A series of measurements is worth more every year, and it can only be started early.
question: What makes the twelve-year record valuable?
why: One season's result is hard to read without knowing how ordinary that season was. A long record says exactly that. It can show this year was unusually dry, or unusually early, which is what explains why some traits paid off now. And it cannot be built later. Last year's cover and flowering are gone. Routine measurements feel pointless in any one year.
answerText: It says how ordinary a season was. And nobody can go back and measure a season that has already gone.

choices: It lets any one season be read against how ordinary it was.
It makes each year's measurements more accurate.
It is required before the trial results can be published.
It removes the need to measure yield at all.
rebuttals: Each year's measurement is as accurate as its instrument, however many years there are.
Nothing about publishing requires it, which is why it is the first thing cut.
Yield still has to be measured. The record explains it rather than replacing it.
